name: Cost Per Computation
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Real Price of a Quantum Answer
lesson.summary: Dividing the enormous infrastructure cost of running a quantum computer by the small number of genuinely useful computations it currently delivers shows quantum computing to be extremely expensive per unit of useful work compared to classical alternatives.
lesson.body:
Cost per computation is a deceptively simple metric: take the total cost of running and maintaining a computing system over some period, and divide it by the number of useful, correct computations it actually delivered in that period. It is the metric that ultimately decides whether a technology is commercially viable, no matter how impressive its peak theoretical capability looks in a research paper, because a customer does not pay for potential, they pay for delivered, usable results.

The numerator, infrastructure cost, is high for quantum hardware for reasons already covered in this chapter. Superconducting qubit systems need dilution refrigerators costing several hundred thousand to over a million dollars apiece, running continuously and consuming meaningful power to hold chips near absolute zero. Trapped-ion and photonic systems instead require precision laser systems, ultra-high vacuum chambers, and cleanroom-grade environmental stability. Layered on top of the raw equipment cost is the scarce, expensive engineering talent needed to keep these systems calibrated, since quantum hardware drifts out of tune far more readily than classical silicon does.

The denominator is where quantum computing's current disadvantage becomes sharper still. Today's devices have high error rates, so a single "answer" often requires many repeated runs, commonly called shots, to statistically extract a usable result, and a meaningful share of attempted jobs must be discarded, corrected, or rerun due to noise. The count of genuinely useful, verified computations a system delivers is therefore small relative to its raw operating time, which pushes the cost-per-computation figure higher from both directions at once: an expensive numerator divided by a shrunken denominator.

A purely illustrative, order-of-magnitude exercise makes the shape of the problem concrete without attaching it to any specific company's disclosed figures. Imagine a modest lab-scale quantum system costing on the order of ten to fifteen million dollars a year to build, maintain, and staff, a plausible range given the hardware and talent costs described above. If that system delivers, in a given year, only a few thousand genuinely useful and independently verifiable computational results after accounting for error and repetition overhead, the implied cost per useful computation lands somewhere in the thousands of dollars. Compare that to equivalent classical cloud workloads, which frequently cost anywhere from a fraction of a cent to a few dollars depending on complexity. This is a hypothetical reasoning exercise, not a reported number from any real company, but it illustrates why the gap between quantum and classical cost per computation is currently measured in orders of magnitude rather than in a modest premium.

This is the quantitative backbone of the previous chapter's more qualitative point about classical alternatives being cheaper: it is not simply that classical computing happens to be more familiar or better supported, it is that the arithmetic of cost divided by useful output currently favors classical computing by a wide margin for almost any workload available today. Cost per computation, though, only captures the compute side of the ledger. The next chapter widens the lens to the full cost of owning a quantum system, facilities, staffing, and integration included.
